questions.q: What three essential components are always required to form a shadow on a surface?
questions.a: A source of light, an opaque or translucent object to block the light, and a screen (or surface) to receive the shadow. A wrong answer reveals that the student confuses shadows with reflections or thinks shadows can exist without a surface to fall upon.

questions.q: Why is a shadow always dark, regardless of whether the object blocking the light is bright red or shiny yellow?
questions.a: A shadow is formed because the object completely blocks light rays from reaching that specific region behind it, resulting in an absence of light (darkness). A wrong answer reveals the misconception that a shadow inherits the color of the object that blocks the light.

questions.q: A student places a cricket ball 20 cm away from a small LED torch (acting as a point source) and projects its shadow on a wall that is 100 cm away from the torch. If the ball has a diameter of 7 cm, calculate the approximate magnification factor if the shadow size depends linearly on the ratio of screen distance to source-to-object distance.
questions.a:
Steps: 
1. Identify given values: Distance from source to object ($d_{so} = 20\text{ cm}$), distance from source to screen ($d_{ss} = 100\text{ cm}$), object size ($h_o = 7\text{ cm}$).
2. Identify the formula for linear magnification ($m$) or shadow size ($h_s$): $h_s = h_o \times \left(\frac{d_{ss}}{d_{so}}\right)$.
3. Substitute values with units: $h_s = 7\text{ cm} \times \left(\frac{100\text{ cm}}{20\text{ cm}}\right)$.
4. Compute and track unit cancellation: $h_s = 7\text{ cm} \times 5 = 35\text{ cm}$.
5. Verify physical reasonableness: The shadow size is larger than the object because the screen is further away than the object, which aligns with geometric optics.
Answer: 35 cm. A wrong answer reveals an error in setting up the ratio of distances or dividing by the wrong distance term.

questions.q: How does replacing a point source of light (like a small LED bulb) with an extended source of light (like a long tube light) affect the appearance of a shadow cast by an opaque sphere?
questions.a: An extended source creates a sharp central dark region called the umbra and a lighter outer fringe called the penumbra, whereas a point source creates only a sharp, uniform umbra. A wrong answer shows a failure to recognize that light rays from different parts of a large source overlap partially to create a faded outer region.

questions.q: A student claims that if you move a screen closer to an opaque object while keeping the light source fixed, the shadow will become larger. Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect because moving the screen closer to the object decreases the spread of the blocked light cone, thereby making the shadow smaller, not larger. A wrong answer indicates confusion between object-to-source distance and screen-to-object distance effects on shadow dimensions.

questions.q: Design a simple home experiment using a torch, a small globe, and a blank wall to demonstrate why shadows change length throughout the day.
questions.a: Criteria for a good answer: The student must describe placing a stationary object (globe) and moving the torch from a low angle (simulating morning/evening) to a high vertical angle (simulating noon), noting how the shadow length decreases and then increases while changing angle. A poor answer lacks clear placement of the light source or fails to link the angle of the light beam to the length of the shadow.
